title: Simplex colimits and product comparison for simplicial realization
statement: Use simplicial sets and standard simplices as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Let $\mathcal K$ be the category of k-spaces (spaces whose topology is final for maps from compact Hausdorff spaces), with k-ified products and small colimits. For every simplicial set $X$, let $\operatorname{Simp}(X)$ be the category whose objects are maps $\Delta^n\to X$ from standard simplices and whose morphisms are commuting maps of standard simplices. The canonical cocone of standard simplices over $\operatorname{Simp}(X)$ is colimiting in simplicial sets. In particular, products of simplicial sets commute with these simplex colimits separately in either variable. Suppose a functor $R:\mathbf{sSet}\to\mathcal K$ preserves small colimits, and suppose that for every $m,n$ the canonical comparison $R(\Delta^m\times\Delta^n)\to R(\Delta^m)\times^{\mathcal K}R(\Delta^n)$ is a homeomorphism. If maps in $\mathcal K$ satisfy the exponential law that continuous maps $k(C\times Y)\to Z$ are naturally in bijection with continuous maps $C\to kC(Y,Z)$ for k-spaces $C,Y,Z$, then the canonical comparison $R(X\times Y)\to R(X)\times^{\mathcal K}R(Y)$ is a homeomorphism for all simplicial sets $X,Y$, naturally in both variables.

proof.text: For $x\in X_n$ define $s_x:\Delta^n\to X$ in degree $r$ by $s_x(\alpha)=X(\alpha)(x)$ for $\alpha:[r]\to[n]$. The functor identities give its naturality. Conversely, any simplicial map $s:\Delta^n\to X$ satisfies $s_r(\alpha)=X(\alpha)(s_n(\mathrm{id}_{[n]}))$, by its naturality at $\alpha$. Thus $x\mapsto s_x$ and $s\mapsto s_n(\mathrm{id})$ are inverse. Applying this also with $X=\Delta^m$, every map between standard simplices is induced by its unique monotone map. Consequently the objects of $\operatorname{Simp}(X)$ are pairs $(n,x)$ and a morphism $(r,z)\to(n,x)$ is precisely an $\alpha:[r]\to[n]$ with $z=X(\alpha)(x)$. This is a small category: the object set is $\coprod_{n\geq0}X_n$, and every hom-set is a subset of the finite set of monotone maps between the two finite ordinals.

source.place: §3.1, definition of the category of simplices and Lemma 3.1.3, printed p.75; explicit evaluation calculation

proof.text: Let $a_{n,x}:\Delta^n\to Z$ be a cocone on this simplex diagram. Define $f_n(x)=(a_{n,x})_n(\mathrm{id}_{[n]})$. For $\alpha:[r]\to[n]$, the cocone equation is $a_{r,X(\alpha)x}=a_{n,x}\circ\Delta(\alpha)$; evaluation at $\mathrm{id}_{[r]}$ gives $f_r(X(\alpha)x)=Z(\alpha)(f_n(x))$. Hence $f:X\to Z$ is simplicial. The evaluation formula of step 1 gives $f\circ s_x=a_{n,x}$ in every degree. Conversely these equations determine $f_n(x)$ by evaluation at the identity, so $f$ is unique. This proves the canonical cocone colimiting by the ordinary categorical universal property. It also covers $X=\varnothing$: the cocone family and the map from the empty simplicial set are both unique.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.3, printed p.75; expansion of its one-sentence proof

proof.text: For a fixed set $T$, ordinary currying and evaluation give inverse bijections $\operatorname{Hom}(T\times B,V)=\operatorname{Hom}(B,V^T)$, natural in $B,V$, where $V^T$ is the set of functions $T\to V$. Thus $T\times-$ is a left adjoint. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-left-adjoint-preserves-colimits] to conclude that it preserves every small set colimit, including the empty one. By [lem-weil-pbc-presheaf-colimits-sectionwise] with indexing category $\Delta$, a small colimit of simplicial sets is formed degreewise in sets. Products are also degreewise by [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. For a fixed simplicial set $B$, the degree-$r$ comparison for $B\times-$ is therefore exactly the just-established comparison for $B_r\times-$ in sets. Its inverses commute with every simplicial operator because the comparison does; hence it is an isomorphism of simplicial sets. Interchanging the two factors gives the assertion in the other variable. In particular both product functors preserve the simplex colimits of step 2.

source.place: Tag 0038, lemma-adjoint-exact (1); sites.tex, Tag 00VB, section-limits-colimits-PSh; degreewise specialization

proof.text: Use the notation $kC(Y,Z)$ and k-ification of [lem-coef-kspace-exponential-law]. First, $kC(Y,Z)$ is a k-space, so the right side lies in $\mathcal K$: the identity $kT\to T$ is continuous since every open set of $T$ passes every compact test, and a compact Hausdorff test $a:C\to T$ is continuous into $kT$ directly from the definition of its open sets; thus $kT$ and $T$ have the same compact tests, whence $k(kT)=kT$. Moreover, for k-spaces $C,Y$ the k-ified product $k(C\times Y)$ is the product $C\times^{\mathcal K}Y$ of the statement. The exponential law assumed in the statement says precisely that $-\times^{\mathcal K}Y$ is left adjoint to $kC(Y,-)$: its hom-set bijections are natural in the source and target. For fixed $Y$ and $g:Z\to Z'$, the right-adjoint action is postcomposition $h\mapsto g\circ h$, as specified by that naturality. Therefore [lem-weil-pbc-left-adjoint-preserves-colimits] shows that $-\times^{\mathcal K}Y$ carries every existing small colimit cocone to a colimit cocone. The symmetry $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$ of the k-ified products gives the same result for $Y\times^{\mathcal K}-$: the ordinary swap and its inverse are continuous, and k-ification preserves their inverse equations. This includes empty diagrams. No product-topology assertion about ordinary, un-k-ified products is required.

source.place: Tag 0038, lemma-adjoint-exact (1), applied to the assumed exponential law; Hovey Proposition 2.4.22(5), printed p.58

proof.text:
Write $q_{B,E}:R(B\times E)\to R(B)\times^{\mathcal K}R(E)$ for the pair of maps $R(\operatorname{pr}_1),R(\operatorname{pr}_2)$. For maps $b:B\to B'$ and $e:E\to E'$, functoriality and the two projection equations imply
$$q_{B',E'}\circ R(b\times e)=(R(b)\times^{\mathcal K}R(e))\circ q_{B,E}.$$
Indeed composing either side with the first projection gives $R(b\circ\operatorname{pr}_1)$ and with the second gives $R(e\circ\operatorname{pr}_2)$. This proves naturality of the actual canonical comparison before constructing any inverse.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.8, printed p.77, canonical comparison; elementary projection calculation

proof.text: Fix $m$ and put $B=\Delta^m$. Index by $(n,y)\in\operatorname{Simp}(Y)$, writing $j_y:\Delta^n\to Y$. By steps 2 and 3, the legs $B\times\Delta^n\to B\times Y$ give a colimit; applying the assumed colimit-preserving $R$ gives a colimit with apex $R(B\times Y)$ and legs $u_y=R(\mathrm{id}_B\times j_y)$. By step 4 and colimit preservation of $R$, the legs $v_y=\mathrm{id}_{R(B)}\times^{\mathcal K}R(j_y)$ give a colimit with apex $R(B)\times^{\mathcal K}R(Y)$. Put $h_y=q_{B,\Delta^n}$, an isomorphism by hypothesis. Step 5 gives naturality of $h_y$ in the simplex index and $q_{B,Y}u_y=v_yh_y$. Therefore the maps $u_yh_y^{-1}$ form a cocone on the second diagram: for any transition $a:i\to j$, naturality gives $h_j^{-1}D'(a)=D(a)h_i^{-1}$, and the cocone equation for $u$ then gives the required equation. The universal property supplies $g$ with $gv_y=u_yh_y^{-1}$. Now $(gq_{B,Y})u_y=u_y$ and $(q_{B,Y}g)v_y=v_y$ for every index. The uniqueness clauses of the two colimits give $gq_{B,Y}=\mathrm{id}$ and $q_{B,Y}g=\mathrm{id}$. Thus $q_{\Delta^m,Y}$ is an isomorphism for every $m,Y$.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.8, first sentence of proof, printed p.77; explicit colimit inverse for a fixed standard simplex

proof.text: Fix an arbitrary $Y$, and index now by $(m,x)\in\operatorname{Simp}(X)$ with legs $i_x:\Delta^m\to X$. Steps 2 and 3 and colimit preservation of $R$ give a colimit with apex $R(X\times Y)$ and legs $u_x=R(i_x\times\mathrm{id}_Y)$. Step 4 gives a colimit with apex $R(X)\times^{\mathcal K}R(Y)$ and legs $v_x=R(i_x)\times^{\mathcal K}\mathrm{id}_{R(Y)}$. By step 6, $h_x=q_{\Delta^m,Y}$ is an isomorphism; step 5 gives $q_{X,Y}u_x=v_xh_x$ and naturality of $h_x$ in this index. Thus the same explicit cocone equation $h_j^{-1}D'(a)=D(a)h_i^{-1}$ shows that $u_xh_x^{-1}$ induces a map $g$ with $gv_x=u_xh_x^{-1}$. Comparing composites with every $u_x$ and $v_x$ gives $gq_{X,Y}=\mathrm{id}$ and $q_{X,Y}g=\mathrm{id}$ by colimit uniqueness. An isomorphism in this category is a continuous map with continuous inverse, hence a homeomorphism. Equation of step 5 proves naturality in both variables; multiplying that equation by the inverses also proves naturality of the inverse. Empty simplex categories cause no exception, since uniqueness of maps out of an initial object is the same empty-family uniqueness clause used here.
